amendments.rule: The postposition `χάριν` takes the whole discontinuous English frame the ASV builds around it — `Τούτου χάριν` → *For this cause*, `αἰσχροῦ κέρδους χάριν` → *for filthy lucre's sake* — as one `aligned` unit headed on the noun, *cause* or *sake*, and the genitive it governs stands alone on its own English word. The English preposition is supplied because no **proper** Greek preposition is present for it to answer to, and the noun is what carries the postposition's sense, so rule 17's meaning-bearing complement decides the head. Rule 45's `διὰ τοῦτο` → *For this cause* is the contrast: there a proper Greek preposition governs the phrase, so *for … cause* belongs to `διά` and is headed on *for* while the demonstrative takes *this*. The test is whether a **proper** Greek preposition is present, not whether the English reads alike, which is why the identical *For this cause* is headed on *cause* for `χάριν` and on *for* for `διά`. An **improper** preposition is not that contrast and reads with `χάριν` rather than with `διά`. Rule 95 fixes the class from the lexeme and never from the morph tag, which marks `ἕνεκα` and `ἕνεκεν` `PREP` exactly as it marks `διά`: a preposition governing one case only and forming no verbal compound is improper, and rule 71 heads its frame on the frame's lexical noun, the English preposition standing in front of it belonging to the idiom rather than answering to the governed case, as rule 42 has it. So `Ἕνεκα τούτου` → *For this cause* is one `aligned` unit headed on *cause*, the demonstrative keeping a bare *this*, exactly as `ἕνεκεν τοῦ ὀνόματός μου` → *for my name's sake* is headed on *sake* under rule 78 and `ἕνεκεν τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ θεοῦ` → *for the kingdom of God's sake* is there. Every corpus unit heading a *for … sake* wrap on the prepositional word carries a proper `διά` or `ὑπέρ`, so not one of them is precedent for an adverb governing a case. Do not read the mere presence of a preposition, or the English reading alike, as licensing a head on *for*: ask first whether the preposition is proper.
amendments.why: MAT.19 met the case rule 46 had not considered. 19:5 `Ἕνεκα τούτου` → *For this cause* is the same English rule 46 uses to contrast `χάριν` with `διά`, but its carrier is an improper preposition — governing the genitive alone, forming no verbal compound, and tagged `PREP` exactly as `διά` is. Rule 46's test as written ("whether a Greek preposition is present") sends that head to *for*, contradicting rules 71, 78 and 95, which head an improper preposition's frame on its lexical noun and name `ἕνεκεν … σake` → on *sake* in terms. Narrowing the test to a **proper** preposition removes the contradiction where it stands rather than leaving the over-broad sentence for the next verse pass to read first. The chapter's own 19:5 (*cause*), 19:29 (*sake*) and 19:12 (`διά` → *for*) are consistent with the amended text, and rule 78's count — every corpus *for … sake* unit heading on the prepositional word carries a proper `διά` or `ὑπέρ` — means no corpus unit contradicts it.

conventions: Where the ASV recasts an oblique Greek pronoun as the subject of its English clause, the pronoun is aligned to that subject word rather than left unrepresented with the English word marked added: σου → *thou* in *sell that which thou hast* at 19:21, and ἡμῖν → *we* in *what then shall we have* at 19:27. Rule 15 permits the reordering; what this settles is that a change of grammatical role is not a change of realization, so no token is emptied and nothing is added.

νεανίσκος → *young man* heads on *young* at 19:20 and 19:22. The *man* is the generic completion rule 66 names and the lexeme's own sense sits in the νεαν- element, as πλεονέκτης → *covetous man* heads on *covetous* and πτωχός → *a poor man* on *poor*. Heading on *man* is conceded in both units.

Rule 32's apposition clause — another source token having already written the antecedent — reaches a nominal standing inside the article's own phrase, not one standing across an expressed copula. ὑμεῖς οἱ ἀκολουθήσαντές → *ye who have followed* at 19:28 empties the article, ὑμεῖς having written the *ye*; but εἷς ἐστιν ὁ ἀγαθός → *One there is who is good* at 19:17 does not, εἷς and ὁ ἀγαθός being the two terms of an expressed copula rather than one phrase, so the article keeps the single relativizer under rule 90 and the adjective takes the supplied copula with its own word under rule 53. The expressed ἐστιν is spent on *there is*, so the *is* of the relative clause is a second, supplied copula.

report: Checked all 54 candidate lemma groups end to end, plus the full dump for `added` and folded-helper units, which the lemma table cannot see. No construction is analysed two ways with nothing in the source to license the difference; patches are empty.

Articles: consistent on both arms of rule 20. The article carries a supplied possessive at 19:5 s007, 19:10 s013, 19:13 s006, 19:15 s003, 19:19 s002 and s005 — in every case because no possessor token stands in its phrase; it is emptied at 19:3 s013, 19:8 s006 and s012, 19:9 s008, 19:19 s009, 19:23 s005 and 19:29 s019 — in every case because an expressed genitive writes the possessive. 19:5 writes one English possessive over father+mother and 19:19 writes two, so 19:5 s010 is unrepresented while both articles of 19:19 are aligned. That is the ASV, not a split.

ὅτι aligned at 19:4 and 19:28 and unrepresented at 19:8, 19:9, 19:23 tracks whether the ASV wrote *that*, which is rule 43's own test. εἰσέρχομαι with an expressed εἰς keeps only the verb word at 19:17, 19:23 and 19:24 (rule 106). προσέρχομαι + dative gives *came* to the verb and *unto him* / *to him* to the pronoun at 19:3 and 19:16 alike. The participle-to-finite juncture *and* sits on the finite verb it introduces at 19:4, 19:15, 19:16 and 19:27 without exception (rule 88).

The supplied comparative/impersonal frame is handled alike at 19:23 and 19:24: the frame's first *for* stays inside the predicate's unit (δυσκόλως → *It is hard for*, εὐκοπώτερόν → *easier for*), no nominative or accusative being able to license it under rule 106, and the repeated *for* at 19:24 t020 rides with the member it introduces under rule 103. 19:24's expressed ἐστιν takes *It is* while 19:23 has no copula token, which accounts for the rest of the difference.

19:24's `added` *to enter* checks out against the variant line: SBLGNT.MAT.19.24.v030 is underdetermined with r01 and r02 remaining and the fallback marked excluded by evidence, the projection carrying an r00-base with no infinitive of entering. Rule 97's note requirements are met in the unit.

The one real finding is a contract defect rather than a chapter defect. Rule 46 states its test as whether *a Greek preposition is present*, and 19:5 Ἕνεκα τούτου → *For this cause* is the case it had not considered: a preposition is present, so rule 46 as written heads on *for*, while rules 71, 78 and 95 head an improper preposition's frame on its lexical noun. The chapter followed 71/78/95 (*cause* at 19:5, *sake* at 19:29, against *for* for the proper διά at 19:12). Returned as an amendment narrowing rule 46 to proper prepositions, not as a new rule, because the over-broad sentence is what a verse pass reads first.

BSB: none of the ten disagreements is an error. Eight are articles the ASV leaves nothing to carry — 19:1 τούς and 19:14 τῶν (determiner slot occupied, rules 38 and 49), 19:12/19:14/19:23/19:24 (no determiner written, rules 21 and 23), 19:23 τοῖς (displaced by αὐτοῦ, rule 20), 19:28 οἱ (rule 32's apposition clause, which that rule says will be reported and is not a correction). The other two are recitative ὅτι at 19:9 (rule 43) and predicative εἰς at 19:5 absorbed into *become one flesh* (rule 36). Nothing was changed to move the aggregate.

Flagged without patching: at 19:17 εἷς ἐστιν ὁ ἀγαθός → *One there is who is good* the article keeps the single relativizer under rule 90, while at 19:28 the article is emptied because ὑμεῖς wrote the antecedent. I judge the difference licensed — 19:28 is one appositional phrase, 19:17 is two terms of an expressed copula — and recorded it as a convention rather than a promotion, having no corpus for a substantival article standing before a bare adjective.
